His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure in the right arm is 130/85 mm Hg. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard in the left paravertebral region. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

enhanced_information: The 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent nosebleeds, fatigue, headaches, and leg pain during running, alongside elevated blood pressure (130/85 mm Hg) and a systolic murmur in the left paravertebral region. These findings suggest a likely diagnosis of coarctation of the aorta, which can lead to systemic hypertension and collateral circulation, potentially causing inferior rib notching due to chronic pressure changes. The elevated blood pressure and symptoms of leg pain during exertion further support this diagnosis. Therefore, the most likely finding upon further evaluation would be inferior rib notching, as it is a classic radiographic sign associated with coarctation of the aorta. Other options, such as pulmonary valve stenosis and left-axis deviation on ECG, are less consistent with the clinical presentation and findings.
analysis: The clinical presentation of the 3-year-old boy suggests a likely diagnosis of coarctation of the aorta. Key findings include recurrent nosebleeds, fatigue, headaches, and leg pain during exertion, alongside significantly elevated blood pressure (130/85 mm Hg) for his age. The presence of a systolic murmur in the left paravertebral region further supports this diagnosis, as it may indicate collateral circulation due to the coarctation. In coarctation of the aorta, the upper body (including the arms) often has higher blood pressure compared to the lower body, which can lead to symptoms such as leg pain during exertion due to decreased perfusion. Over time, the increased pressure can cause changes in the ribs, specifically inferior rib notching, due to erosion from the collateral circulation. This is a classic radiographic finding associated with chronic coarctation of the aorta. Other options, such as pulmonary valve stenosis and left-axis deviation on ECG, do not align as closely with the clinical picture. Therefore, the most likely finding upon further evaluation would be inferior rib notching, which is consistent with the expected complications of coarctation of the aorta. Thus, the best-supported option is 'inferior rib notching'.
